title: Natural Language Processing Fundamentals
summary: Explain tokenisation and why text must be converted to numbers before any model can process it.
objectives: Tokenise text with a provided tokeniser
Read a token list and its numeric ids
Spot sub-word splits of long or rare words
Explain why text becomes numbers before a model can use it

segments.title: What you will build
segments.body:
## What you will build

A model cannot read letters; it works with numbers. A tokeniser splits text into pieces called tokens and gives every piece a number, its id. In this lab you write three sentences of your own and run them through the lab's tokeniser, `tokenize` from `labmock`. You print the tokens and the ids for each sentence, then collect every word that was split into smaller pieces in a list called `surprising_splits`. Those splits show how a model copes with long or rare words: it builds them from smaller parts it already knows.

lab.title: Tokenise your own sentences
lab.objective: Run three sentences of your own through the lab tokeniser, print the tokens and their ids, and collect the words that were split into sub-word pieces.
lab.instructions:
The lab tokeniser is tokenize from labmock (from labmock import tokenize). tokenize("AI is powerful") returns a list of dictionaries, one per token: [{"token": "AI", "id": ...}, {"token": "is", "id": ...}, {"token": "powe", "id": ...}, {"token": "##rful", "id": ...}]. A piece that starts with ## continues the word before it. The id is a number from a fixed vocabulary: the same piece always gets the same id.

1. Fill in sentence_1, sentence_2 and sentence_3 with three different sentences of your own, at least 4 words each. Use plain words, spaces and a full stop (no hyphens or apostrophes), and include at least one long word so that something gets split.
2. For each sentence, call tokenize(sentence). Make a list of the token strings and a list of the ids. Print three lines: Sentence: <the sentence>, Tokens: <list of token strings>, IDs: <list of ids>. Append the token list to token_lists and the id list to id_lists, so each holds three lists in sentence order.
3. Find the surprising splits: for every word in every sentence, remove end punctuation with word.strip(".,!?") and call tokenize(word). If it returns more than one token, the word was broken into pieces: add the word to the list surprising_splits.
4. Print Split words: followed by surprising_splits, and Total tokens: followed by the total number of tokens in all three sentences.

Example lines for the sentence "AI is powerful.":
Tokens: ['AI', 'is', 'powe', '##rful', '.']
Split words: ['powerful']
lab.constraints: Use tokenize from labmock for every token and id; do not split text yourself. Keep the names sentence_1, sentence_2, sentence_3, token_lists, id_lists and surprising_splits. Sentences must be your own, different from each other, at least 4 words each. No input().
lab.starter_code:
from labmock import tokenize

# 1. Write three different sentences of your own, at least 4 words each. Use plain words, spaces
#    and a full stop (no hyphens or apostrophes). Make sure at least one word is longer than
#    5 letters, for example "powerful" or "unbelievable".
sentence_1 = ""
sentence_2 = ""
sentence_3 = ""
sentences = [sentence_1, sentence_2, sentence_3]

# 2. For each sentence: tokens = tokenize(sentence) gives a list of dicts like
#    {"token": "powe", "id": 12345}. Build the list of token strings and the list of ids.
#    Print "Sentence:", then "Tokens:" followed by the token list, then "IDs:" followed by the ids.
#    Append the token list to token_lists and the id list to id_lists.
token_lists = []
id_lists = []


# 3. Find the words that were split: for each word in each sentence, strip punctuation with
#    word.strip(".,!?") and call tokenize(word). If it gives MORE than one token, the word was
#    split into sub-word pieces: add the word to surprising_splits.
surprising_splits = []


# 4. Print "Split words:" followed by surprising_splits, and "Total tokens:" followed by the
#    total number of tokens across the three sentences.
hints: tokenize(sentence) gives a list of dicts. A list comprehension pulls out one key: pieces = [t["token"] for t in tokens] and ids = [t["id"] for t in tokens].
Loop with for sentence in sentences: inside, print the three lines and then token_lists.append(pieces) and id_lists.append(ids).

For the splits use two loops: for sentence in sentences: for word in sentence.split(): word = word.strip(".,!?") and then if len(tokenize(word)) > 1: surprising_splits.append(word). The total is sum(len(p) for p in token_lists).

visible_examples.description: A long word is split into 4-letter pieces
The same piece always gets the same id
visible_examples.code:
from labmock import tokenize

a = tokenize("cake")[0]["id"]
b = tokenize("I like cake")[2]["id"]
print(a == b)
print(len(tokenize("unbelievable")))

success_criteria: sentence_1, sentence_2 and sentence_3 are three different sentences of at least 4 words each
token_lists holds the token strings of each sentence, exactly as tokenize() returns them
Your output has a Tokens: line for each sentence
id_lists holds the ids of each sentence, exactly as tokenize() returns them
surprising_splits lists every word from your sentences that the tokeniser broke into pieces (at least one)

tests.label: Three different sentences of at least 4 words
tests.remediation: Put your own sentences in sentence_1, sentence_2 and sentence_3 (strings of at least 4 words, all different).

definition.expr: all(isinstance(s, str) and len(s.split()) >= 4 for s in [sentence_1, sentence_2, sentence_3]) and len({sentence_1, sentence_2, sentence_3}) == 3

tests.label: token_lists matches tokenize() for your sentences
tests.remediation: token_lists must hold three lists (one per sentence, in order) of the "token" strings from tokenize(sentence).
tests.objective: Tokenise text with a provided tokeniser

definition.expr: token_lists == [[t['token'] for t in __import__('labmock').tokenize(s)] for s in [sentence_1, sentence_2, sentence_3]]

tests.label: A Tokens: line is printed for each sentence
tests.remediation: Print "Tokens:" followed by the list of token strings for every sentence, for example print("Tokens:", pieces).

tests.label: id_lists matches the ids from tokenize()
tests.remediation: id_lists must hold three lists (one per sentence, in order) of the "id" numbers from tokenize(sentence).

tests.label: surprising_splits holds exactly the words that were split
tests.remediation: For every word of every sentence, strip punctuation with word.strip(".,!?") and add it to surprising_splits only if tokenize(word) gives more than one token. At least one sentence needs a word longer than 5 letters.

lab.solution:
from labmock import tokenize

sentence_1 = "Tokenisation is surprisingly powerful."
sentence_2 = "My grandmother bakes unbelievable chocolate cake."
sentence_3 = "The model reads numbers, not words."
sentences = [sentence_1, sentence_2, sentence_3]

token_lists = []
id_lists = []
for sentence in sentences:
    tokens = tokenize(sentence)
    pieces = [t["token"] for t in tokens]
    ids = [t["id"] for t in tokens]
    token_lists.append(pieces)
    id_lists.append(ids)
    print("Sentence:", sentence)
    print("Tokens:", pieces)
    print("IDs:", ids)

surprising_splits = []
for sentence in sentences:
    for word in sentence.split():
        word = word.strip(".,!?")
        if len(tokenize(word)) > 1:
            surprising_splits.append(word)

print("Split words:", surprising_splits)
print("Total tokens:", sum(len(pieces) for pieces in token_lists))
